questions.question: What is the fundamental electronic event when a nucleophile attacks the carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone?

options.label: A
options.text: The nucleophile donates electrons into the C-C σ bond.

options.label: B
options.text: The nucleophile donates an electron pair into the empty π* antibonding orbital of the carbonyl carbon, breaking the C=O π bond and pushing electrons onto oxygen.

options.label: C
options.text: The carbonyl carbon is oxidized to a radical cation.

options.label: D
options.text: Oxygen donates a lone pair to the nucleophile.

questions.correct_answer: The nucleophile donates an electron pair into the empty π* antibonding orbital of the carbonyl carbon, breaking the C=O π bond and pushing electrons onto oxygen.
questions.explanation: Nucleophiles attack the electrophilic π* orbital at the Bürgi-Dunitz angle (~107°), generating a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.

questions.question: What is the key resonance-stabilized intermediate in the acid-catalyzed conversion of a hemiacetal to an acetal?

options.label: A
options.text: A tetrahedral carbanion.

options.label: B
options.text: An enol ether radical.

options.label: C
options.text: An oxocarbenium ion [R-CH=O⁺-R' ↔ R-C⁺H-O-R'] formed by protonation and loss of water from the hemiacetal.

options.label: D
options.text: A free carbocation with an empty octet on all atoms.

questions.correct_answer: An oxocarbenium ion [R-CH=O⁺-R' ↔ R-C⁺H-O-R'] formed by protonation and loss of water from the hemiacetal.
questions.explanation: Protonation of the hemiacetal -OH allows loss of water, generating a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion that is trapped by a second alcohol.

questions.question: Why does the formation of an imine from cyclohexanone and primary amine exhibit a maximum rate at pH 4.5?

options.label: A
options.text: pH 4.5 is the boiling point of the solvent.

options.label: B
options.text: At pH 4.5, there is sufficient acid to protonate the carbinolamine -OH for dehydration (RDS) while leaving enough unprotonated free amine nucleophile to initiate attack.

options.label: C
options.text: At higher pH, the imine decomposes to an alkane.

options.label: D
options.text: At lower pH, the aldehyde is completely destroyed.

questions.correct_answer: At pH 4.5, there is sufficient acid to protonate the carbinolamine -OH for dehydration (RDS) while leaving enough unprotonated free amine nucleophile to initiate attack.
questions.explanation: A delicate acid-base balance is required: too acidic protonates all amine (no nucleophile); too basic prevents protonation of -OH (no dehydration leaving group).

questions.question: Why do secondary amines react with ketones to form enamines rather than imines?

options.label: A
options.text: Enamines are aromatic compounds.

options.label: B
options.text: Secondary amines are too bulky to form C=N bonds.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the carbinolamine intermediate lacks a proton on nitrogen; loss of a proton from the adjacent α-carbon is required to eliminate water and achieve neutrality.

options.label: D
options.text: Secondary amines oxidize ketones to esters.

questions.correct_answer: Because the carbinolamine intermediate lacks a proton on nitrogen; loss of a proton from the adjacent α-carbon is required to eliminate water and achieve neutrality.
questions.explanation: Lacking a second N-H proton, the intermediate must lose an α-proton to form the neutral C=C-N enamine system.

questions.question: What is the driving force and final product of the Wolff-Kishner reduction of hydrazones in hot base?

options.label: A
options.text: Homolytic cleavage of the C-N bond by UV light.

options.label: B
options.text: Oxidation of the hydrazone to an amide.

options.label: C
options.text: Reduction of the hydrazone by potassium metal.

options.label: D
options.text: Sequential deprotonation and tautomerization of the hydrazone intermediate drives irreversible elimination of exceptionally stable N₂ gas, yielding an alkane.

questions.correct_answer: Sequential deprotonation and tautomerization of the hydrazone intermediate drives irreversible elimination of exceptionally stable N₂ gas, yielding an alkane.
questions.explanation: The immense thermodynamic stability of elemental nitrogen gas (N≡N bond energy ~945 kJ/mol) drives the reduction to completion.

questions.question: What is the structure of the cyclic intermediate in the Wittig reaction between an aldehyde and a phosphonium ylide?

options.label: A
options.text: A four-membered cyclic oxaphosphetane intermediate formed by [2+2] cycloaddition, which rapidly collapses to form an alkene and triphenylphosphine oxide (Ph₃P=O).

options.label: B
options.text: A planar five-membered phospholane.

options.label: C
options.text: A six-membered cyclic betaine diester.

options.label: D
options.text: A three-membered epoxide ring.

questions.correct_answer: A four-membered cyclic oxaphosphetane intermediate formed by [2+2] cycloaddition, which rapidly collapses to form an alkene and triphenylphosphine oxide (Ph₃P=O).
questions.explanation: The reaction proceeds via a 4-membered oxaphosphetane ring whose collapse is driven by the enormous strength of the P=O bond (~540 kJ/mol).

questions.question: What is the stereochemical outcome at the migrating center during a Baeyer-Villiger oxidation of a chiral ketone?

options.label: A
options.text: The migrating center is oxidized to an alcohol.

options.label: B
options.text: The migrating center undergoes 100% inversion.

options.label: C
options.text: The migrating group shifts to oxygen with complete retention of stereochemical configuration, proceeding through a concerted tetrahedral Criegee intermediate.

options.label: D
options.text: The migrating center racemizes completely via a free carbocation.

questions.correct_answer: The migrating group shifts to oxygen with complete retention of stereochemical configuration, proceeding through a concerted tetrahedral Criegee intermediate.
questions.explanation: Migration occurs with complete retention because the alkyl group migrates with its bonding electron pair in a concerted frontside shift.

questions.question: Why is cyanohydrin formation from acetone and NaCN/H⁺ reversible upon addition of strong aqueous base?

options.label: A
options.text: Base oxidizes the nitrile to a carboxylic acid.

options.label: B
options.text: Cyanide evaporates as nitrogen gas.

options.label: C
options.text: Base deprotonates the hydroxyl group, generating an alkoxide that expels cyanide ion (an acceptable leaving group) to regenerate the carbonyl group.

options.label: D
options.text: The cyanohydrin undergoes a 1,2-alkyl shift.

questions.correct_answer: Base deprotonates the hydroxyl group, generating an alkoxide that expels cyanide ion (an acceptable leaving group) to regenerate the carbonyl group.
questions.explanation: Deprotonation of the -OH group triggers reform of the stable C=O π bond with expulsion of cyanide as a leaving group.

questions.question: What is the curved-arrow description of the reduction of an aldehyde by sodium borohydride (NaBH₄)?

options.label: A
options.text: A nucleophilic hydride ion is transferred from the B-H σ bond directly to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, with simultaneous cleavage of the C=O π bond to oxygen.

options.label: B
options.text: Sodium transfers an electron to the carbonyl carbon.

options.label: C
options.text: Free hydride ions (H⁻) float freely in solution before attacking.

options.label: D
options.text: Boron attacks the carbonyl oxygen directly.

questions.correct_answer: A nucleophilic hydride ion is transferred from the B-H σ bond directly to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, with simultaneous cleavage of the C=O π bond to oxygen.
questions.explanation: NaBH₄ transfers a hydride directly from the B-H bond into the carbonyl π* orbital in a concerted bimolecular step.

questions.question: Why does diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL-H) at -78°C reduce esters cleanly to aldehydes without overreduction to alcohols?

options.label: A
options.text: The bulky tetrahedral hemiacetal aluminate intermediate is stable at -78°C and does not collapse to the aldehyde until aqueous workup destroys remaining hydride.

options.label: B
options.text: DIBAL-H cannot reduce aldehydes under any conditions.

options.label: C
options.text: The ester is oxidized to a peracid.

options.label: D
options.text: The alcohol byproduct inhibits the reaction.

questions.correct_answer: The bulky tetrahedral hemiacetal aluminate intermediate is stable at -78°C and does not collapse to the aldehyde until aqueous workup destroys remaining hydride.
questions.explanation: At -78°C, the tetrahedral intermediate is stable and cannot release the aldehyde into solution where excess hydride could reduce it.

questions.question: Why does the formation of an imine from cyclohexanone and primary amine exhibit a maximum rate at pH 4.5?
